articles.title: Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
articles.snippet: Ukraine says the missile and drone attack on the strategic bridge in the Russian-annexed Crimea took weeks to plan.
articles.full_text:
Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
- Published
Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge has collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Moscow's war effort.
The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before" and that Russian President Vladimir Putin had been briefed on the overnight attack.
Elsewhere, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges - key crossings over the Dnipro River - had been closed after Russia hit Ukraine's capital overnight.
The Southern bridge partially reopened on Tuesday, Klitschko said.
Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.
While Kyiv has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.
The Crimean Bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and illegally annexed Ukraine's southern peninsula in 2014.
The $3.6bn (Â£2.7bn) piece of infrastructure is widely seen in Russia and Ukraine as Putin's personal pet project: His close tycoon friend Arkady Rotenberg built it, and then Putin personally opened it by driving a lorry over it in May 2018.
In Ukraine, the much-hated bridge is seen as one of the main symbols of Russia's continuing occupation of Ukrainian lands.
"We're drinking champagne!" Andrii, an engineer who lives in Kyiv, told the BBC.
He said the latest attack would "deal a very heavy blow to the morale of the Russians".
Some Ukrainians are concerned that Putin might now respond by carrying out even more attacks against civilian infrastructure, but Andrii said: "I don't think the Russians can make things much worse; they're already pounding us every single night with everything they've got."
The damage after the overnight attack, involving cruise missiles and drones, appeared to be far more severe than during previous strikes on the bridge, with a large arched section apparently destroyed.
Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.
Zelensky said the strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".
He said several types of Ukrainian drones as well as the country's Flamingo and Neptune cruise missiles were fired overnight during a "pivotal stage".
The Ukrainian president also said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and Russia's transport ministry later said some rail services resumed.
Ukraine's state security service SBU said its operations had "systematically suppressed enemy air defence systems" over a month, and said it showed "no Russian defence systems can guarantee the safety of illegal objects occupied by the invaders".
Meanwhile, Ukraine's military said the roadway on the bridge is "out of action", with no vehicle able to cross it, and the railway section is still standing, but with a damaged arch.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.
Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".
For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry.
Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.
In Kyiv, loud explosions were heard just before midnight on Monday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water supplies.
On Tuesday, Zelensky said four ballistic missiles had targeted the Southern Bridge, and another three had been fired on the Northern Bridge.
Some of Kyiv's above-ground metro services were also damaged in the overnight attacks, local officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.
Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River, connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.
Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the central Cherkasy region, according to local officials.
The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear, though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.
The collapse of the arched section has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia â at least until the crossing can be repaired.
However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of Ukraine's southern Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Kyiv has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.
This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.
There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait, which connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Azov. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.
Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.
In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge â particularly its enormous arch â may have blocked the shipping channel.
This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for the Russian-occupied ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdyansk.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.
Additional reporting by Jaroslav Lukiv

articles.title: How the attack on Crimean Bridge unfolded
articles.snippet: One of the key symbols of Russia's occupation of Ukraine has suffered major damage after a seven-stage attack by Kyiv.
articles.full_text:
How the attack on Putin's prized Crimean Bridge unfolded
- Published
Stretching across the Kerch Strait in the Black Sea, the Crimean Bridge was always a symbol: for Russia, a prestige project cementing its claim to sovereign Ukrainian territory, and for Ukraine, a hated piece of infrastructure emblematic of Moscow's occupation of the Crimean Peninsula.
A key section of the double-arched, 12-mile-long bridge now lies on the seabed, brought down by an arsenal of Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a dramatic collapse.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said that the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".
But eight years after its unveiling, the bridge has now become material proof of Kyiv's ability to pierce through Moscow's military defences to hit even its most treasured and protected structures.
How did the seven-stage operation play out?
The attack on the strategic Crimean Bridge was carried out gradually to cut across several layers of defence, Kyiv confirmed on Tuesday.
For several weeks Ukraine's Security Service and its General Staff gradually destroyed air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare assets, and other designated targets, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
A significant strike had already been reported on 16 November, when drones hit the bridge at night. Traffic was paused briefly then reinstated, and although the arch over the road section was visibly damaged, the structure remained standing.
But that hit turned out to have been only the penultimate stage of a complex attack.
In the early hours of 17 November, the final strikes dealt a fatal blow to the weakened arch structure.
One verified video - filmed from a camera on board a Ukrainian-made Flamingo missile - shows the weapon approaching the main span of the bridge and heading towards the steel arches, with the footage freezing just before impact.
The Flamingo had potentially been modified to be controlled remotely, which improved its accuracy enough to strike the bridge supports, munitions expert Justin Bronk, from the Royal United Services Institute said.
The missile's "very heavy warhead" made it "more suitable" for attacking the bridge's reinforced concrete spans and supports, Bronk added.
Zelensky later confirmed that several types of missiles and drones had been employed in the attack, which led the massive road arch - weighing thousands of tonnes and measuring about 227m in length - to collapse into the strait.
Daylight images taken from the shores of Crimea to the north show a section about 200m (660ft) long of the tarmac was too dragged below into the sea.
This is clearly critical damage to the crossing. Far from just being a decorative feature of the bridge, the arch played a structural role, transferring loads and supporting the span and helping to ensure the stability of the entire structure.
The parallel arch supporting the railway section has remained standing, although it may also have been damaged. All traffic on the bridge was initially suspended, though trains were later allowed to resume running.
But the damage to the bridge's main span is "catastrophic", Colin Capriani, a structural engineer from Monash University in Melbourne, Australia, told BBC Verify. It was "very hard to envisage" how the bridge could be rebuilt given it is clearly well within range of Ukrainian weaponry, Capriani added.
Major attacks in 2022 and 2023 had already caused serious damage to the road spans of the bridge, but the structure survived.
The difference this time is "the most critical and vulnerable part of the bridge has been hit", said David MacKenzie of engineering consultancy COWI, adding that "although the wreckage of the bridge can be cleared fairly quickly, reinstating full road traffic will take over a year".
What effect could the collapse of the bridge have on Crimea?
Moscow uses Crimea as a military base, with airbases, troop concentrations, training grounds and artillery stockpiles. From there it also carries out strikes on the rest of the country and resupplies its troops in southern Ukraine.
The attack comes after a summer of frequent strikes on Crimea, dictated by Ukraine's stated goal of cutting the peninsula off from Russia. At the time, Kyiv vowed to turn the Crimean Peninsula "into an island".
Now - although it is too early to speak of a complete blockade of Crimea â the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis has increased significantly.
There is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions. However, Ukraine has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar, which has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.
Moscow can also still utilise the ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited - and anything on the Black Sea has become vulnerable to attack. Resupplying Crimea by sea is risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.
In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge - particularly its enormous arch - may have blocked the shipping channel. This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for ports in the Sea of Azov, including the occupied cities of Mariupol and Berdyansk.
Away from the operational value of the damage to the bridge, the symbolic significance remains.
In 2018, Putin triumphantly drove over the bridge representing the unification of Russia and Crimea in a Russian-made truck. That section of the road now lays on the seabed.
Nearly five years since he launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Putin continues to wreak destruction on Ukraine's civilian population, but his most prized symbols of power are increasingly threatened by Kyiv's reach.

articles.title: Jensen Huang says he would be 'honoured' to return as Nvidia CEO if board asked him
articles.snippet: Huang says he has had an "outpouring" of calls from investors and others calling for him to return.
articles.full_text:
Jensen Huang says he would be 'honoured' to return as Nvidia CEO if board asked him
- Published
Jensen Huang said he would be "honoured" to return as the boss of tech giant Nvidia if the board asked him to, in his first public comments since his shock resignation.
"I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely," Huang said on X, days after reports he had extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy.
He said he had an "outpouring" of calls from company employees, investors and others calling for him to return as CEO of Nvidia.
But, as the BBC reported on Monday, Nvidia's board is not considering bringing him back to lead the company.
The prospect of Huang returning at this point looks unlikely.
The company's board is investigating his conduct, which includes an alleged affair with an Nvidia executive.
The AI chip giant is set to report its financial results later on Tuesday, during which the company's interim chief executive, Collette Kress, may address the situation with Huang.
Beyond the internal Nvidia investigation, Huang's affair with a woman suspected of being an asset for Beijing is set to see the billionaire questioned before multiple committees of US lawmakers in the weeks ahead.
The Nvidia founder said he had "made serious mistakes in my personal life".
Nonetheless, Huang's statement appeared to show some hope he would be able to move past the major corporate scandal.
Huang said people have continued to "reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics".
"If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang added.
Many technology executives in recent days have praised Huang's role in the artificial intelligence boom. A petition began circulating online over the weekend calling for his reinstatement at the company.
Yet, by Monday, many executives were not openly calling for Huang's return.
Brad Gerstner, a major tech investor who knows Huang personally and also holds a significant stake in Nvidia, last week wrote an open letter saying that Nvidia could consider Huang's reinstatement.
On Monday, Gerstner said during an event hosted by Semafor that his letter had been misunderstood and the investigation into Huang's conduct needed to run its course.
While Gerstner questioned the facts around Huang's departure, he added: "I don't know to what degree he misled the board. If I was on a board I would take that very seriously. Let's be clear no one is above the law."

articles.title: Trump lands in Asia ahead of talks with Russian and Chinese presidents
articles.snippet: The US president said he would be open to a one-on-one meeting with Russia's Vladimir Putin "if it's available".
articles.full_text:
Trump lands in Asia ahead of talks with Russian and Chinese presidents
- Published
President Trump has arrived in the Philippines' capital on the first leg of a trip to Asia, which will end in a meeting in China with its President Xi Jinping and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin.
A red carpet was rolled out for Trump as he walked off Air Force One in Manila. A band played one of his favourite songs, Y.M.C.A., before he was whisked away by helicopter to a hotel.
Trump's first meeting at the Asean Summit was with America's partners in the Quad - India's Narendra Modi, whom he described as a "very tough man", Japan's Sanae Takaichi, who "may be even tougher", and Australia's Anthony Albanese.
"Our countries are the four corners of the free, open, stable, prosperous Indo-Pacific," the US president said.
"We have outstanding relationships and co-ordinate closely... my phone is always open," Trump added.
Many countries in South East Asia have been hit hard by Donald Trump's tariffs and his war on Iran - but their exports to the US rose 30% last year thanks to the AI boom for which the region manufactures many of the components.
The US is hoping to draw more countries here into its "Pax Silica" tech and AI ecosystem, and away from China.
But China's huge influence in this region cannot easily be challenged, and certainly not in the few hours Trump is in the Philippines.
After an overnight stay in Manila, the US president will fly to Shenzhen in China to attend a summit of Asia Pacific leaders and have nuclear talks with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
Asked if he would also be open to a one-on-one meeting with Putin, Trump said: "If it's available, I would".

articles.title: US loses measles elimination status after 26 years amid record case numbers
articles.snippet: States have reported over 5,400 cases and 10 measles-related deaths for the first time since the early 1990s.
articles.full_text:
US loses measles elimination status after 26 years amid record case numbers
- Published
After more than two decades, the US has lost its measles-free status, following two years of record case numbers and deaths.
The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a specialised service of the United Nations, determined the US has had uninterrupted transmission of the same strain of measles for more than 12 months.
Dr Jarbas Barbosa, director of PAHO, announced that Mexico and Bolivia have also lost their measles elimination status, attributing the resurgence in the region to persistent "gaps in vaccination".
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said it was committed to "regaining measles elimination status" by expanding access to vaccines.
The US has seen 5,400 cases of measles this year alone, with 10 measles-related deaths, the most the country has seen since the 1990s.
The measles virus - with its signature blotchy red rash - used to infect millions of children a year before a vaccine was invented. The extremely contagious virus can be fatal, and some patients can experience long-term complications including encephalitis and immune amnesia, which resets the immune system, leaving it with only limited ability to respond to new infections.
The US recommends two measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) shots for children between ages one and six, which is 97% effective in protecting against the illness.
PAHO, a group within the World Health Organization, revoked the US's measles-elimination after determining that the virus had circulated nonstop for more than a year.
"These figures are a serious warning for our region," PAHO's director Barbosa said at a news conference on Tuesday. "Measles is resurging globally amid persistent gaps in vaccination."
He added that Canada, which lost its status of having eliminated measles last year after seeing several large outbreaks, has made strides this year to interrupt transmission.
Daniel Salas, the executive manager of immunisations at PAHO, said that the US and others who lost elimination status would be required to submit corrective action plans outlining how they would attempt to improve vaccination rates.
US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr Kennedy has attempted to make a series of sweeping changes to US vaccine recommendations and policies. The vaccine sceptic has also frequently cast doubt on the safety of MMR shot, as vaccination rates have declined across the US in recent years.
Kennedy has argued that the rise in measles cases started before he took the helm at HHS and that neighbouring countries have also seen more infections.
Responding to Tuesday's announcement, the CDC said the agency and its partners were "committed to stopping measles outbreaks, protecting Americans, and regaining measles elimination status".
"Together, we will encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to vaccines, and help communities close gaps in protection," the agency said.
CDC Director Erica Schwartz said the measles elimination designation was not what protected Americans.
"Vaccination does," she said. "We know where transmission is occurring and we've invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities."
The UK, Spain and Austria were among European nations that lost their measles-free status earlier this year, along with countries including Russia, Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan.
Nuwan Gunawardhana, an assistant professor of medicine with Columbia University Irving Medical Center, said the US losing its elimination status was "a huge leap backwards".
The US was the first country to eliminate measles in the Americas thanks to vaccination campaigns, noted William Moss, a paediatric infectious disease specialist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.
Dr Gunawardhana said it took massive efforts from public health officials and clinicians to build trust with patients to increase uptake of the MMR vaccine, leading to decades in the US with few infections and deaths.
But that trust has been steadily eroding since the Covid-19 pandemic, when Dr Gunawardhana said patients were confronted with misinformation about the safety of vaccines and lost even more trust in public health systems.
The vaccination rate for MMR across the US has fallen to 92.4%, below the 95% level that provides herd immunity, which limits the spread of measles and protects those who cannot get vaccinated, including newborns.
An outbreak in Pennsylvania has infected over 1,400 people - likely a large underestimate - and killed seven people, according to state officials.
Kennedy, the health secretary, has sparred with Pennsylvania officials over how it is counting the measles deaths, with CDC declining for now to record some of the deaths in its database.
Last year, the health secretary fired all the members of a top vaccine advisory panel and replaced them with his own appointees, some of whom were vaccine critics.
The panel recommended a number of vaccine changes - including no longer requiring the Hepatitis B vaccine for all newborns - but those recommendations were blocked by a federal judge.
President Donald Trump this year also cast doubt on the safety of the MMR vaccine, issuing an executive order for the shot to be split into three separate immunisations for measles, mumps and rubella, a move public health experts say is costly and could sow confusion about an already safe vaccine.
Doctors and public health officials say the misinformation from Kennedy and Trump has played a major role in falling vaccination rates.
"It's confusing patients. It's confusing families," Dr Gunawardhana said. "We need a clear message from the top."
The federal government's vaccine manoeuvres have left public health officials and states to fill in the gaps, offering their own separate recommendations upholding decades-long practices.

articles.title: Palestinian woman, 72, shot dead by Israeli settlers in West Bank, health ministry says
articles.snippet: Palestinians say there was an attack by settlers in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, while the Israeli military says the settlers fired after being attacked.
articles.full_text:
Palestinian woman, 72, shot dead by Israeli settlers in West Bank, health ministry says
- Published
A Palestinian woman in her 70s has been shot dead, and several other people wounded, in a village in the occupied West Bank where Israeli settlers recently moved in, the Palestinian health ministry says.
There are conflicting accounts of what happened. Local Palestinians said there was an attack by settlers in part of al-Duyuk al-Tahta, near Jericho, which is meant to be under the full control of the Palestinian Authority.
According to the Israeli army, there was a Palestinian car-ramming attack on an Israeli vehicle. It said rocks were then thrown at the Israelis, who opened fire in response. It did not mention the fatal shooting of a woman.
There have been high tensions in the area since a group of settlers recently set up a new outpost.
They moved into eight houses in the village on 4 November after buying them, they have said, in a secretive operation. The properties are in an area where Israel retains full security control.
All settlements are illegal under international law.
Local Palestinians said that the events in al-Duyuk al-Tahta on Monday night began with harassment by Israeli settlers. Children threw stones, they said, and the settlers opened fire, killing Fadda al-Fahidat, who was 72, outside her home.
According to Palestinian accounts, her son rushed to the scene in his car after hearing the news and collided with an empty Israeli settler car parked outside his family home, injuring settlers who were standing nearby. The settlers then fired more shots, they said.
The statement from the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said that "terrorists accelerated their vehicle toward an Israeli vehicle and rammed it", and then "exited their vehicle with weapons and attacked and harmed the occupants of the Israeli vehicle".
Afterwards, it said, "rocks were hurled at the Israelis, who responded by firing in order to remove the threat."
The IDF said that Israeli security forces were sent to the scene and were pursuing suspects.
Doctors at a hospital in Jericho said that al-Fahidat was shot in the head. Several other Palestinians and Israelis were injured, reports said.
The Israeli human rights group B'Tselem says there has been a prolonged campaign of settler attacks, intimidation and land seizures in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, with Israeli troops now stationed nearby to secure the new settlement.
Residents and activists say armed settlers walk and drive quad bikes around the neighbourhood as they threaten Palestinian residents.
In a separate incident on Monday evening, eight Palestinians were injured when they were hit by a vehicle driven by an Israeli settler on a main road in Tuqu, south of Bethlehem, according to Palestinian officials and the Palestinian Red Crescent.
The IDF said the incident was a traffic accident. But the Palestinian foreign ministry called it a "terrorist attack", saying the driver hit a group of Palestinians who had gathered near the scene of an earlier traffic accident.
Also on Monday, the Civil Administration - the body that implements Israeli government policy in the West Bank - announced the allocation of more than 28 sq km (6,945 acres) of land in the northern Jordan Valley to nine settlers for grazing, according to the Israeli anti-settlement watchdog Peace Now.
It said handing over vast tracts of land to settlers for grazing outposts constituted "direct support for the systematic expulsion of Palestinians from their lands and the rampant criminal violence in the West Bank".
The UK government said on Tuesday that it was imposing sanctions on eight companies building Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
It is the first sanctions package since Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's pledge in September to respond to the accelerating rate of settlement expansion in the West Bank, which he said risked rendering a two-state solution unviable.

articles.title: 'It was really scary': Mother describes sheltering during Russia strikes on Kyiv bridge
articles.snippet: Moscow has targeted bridges in Kyiv, while Ukraine severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea.
articles.full_text:
'It was really scary': Mother describes sheltering during Russia strikes on Kyiv bridge
- Published
The alarms warning of a ballistic missile threat went off just before 23:30 on Monday in Kyiv. Moments later came the boom of explosions.
Once again, the main bridges over the broad River Dnipro that cuts through the city were the target and this time the Russian missiles hit what they wanted.
Close to one end of the Pivnichnyi (Northern) bridge there is a large crater and in the pouring rain, water now rushes through it to the river below. Chunks of tarmac and metal are scattered around.
At its broadest point, the jagged hole is about eight metres wide.
The crossing is closed to all traffic apart from the occasional fire engine or police car passing at high speed. By contrast, nearby roads are jammed with cars and trucks, forced to take long detours.
Anyone in a hurry to move around this city has to walk, or cycle, across the bridge, picking their way through the wreckage. In the miserable weather, that also means getting very wet.
Masha and her family moved to a flat next to the bridge because they had been living by a power plant that kept getting hit by Russian missiles.
Last night, she was in the kitchen of their new place when the Russians struck the bridge. She thought her windows would be blown out of their frames by the explosions.
"It was really scary. We had no idea they'd hit here so much. It's like we're cursed," Masha told me, describing grabbing her child and running into the corridor for protection.
But somehow, she still managed to sound cheerful.
"It's difficult, but we're used to it. And we try to take the positive from everything. Like: we survived today! So we can be happy about that."
From the damage, it looks like Russia targeted the same spot on the bridge with a volley of three missiles, aiming to keep the road closed for as long as possible.
A major recovery operation is under way, with firefighters and engineers in fluorescent overalls working to evaluate the extent of the damage. But it looks like the disruption will continue for some time.
Further along the Dnipro River, the Pivdennyi (Southern) bridge was also hit on Monday night, with four missiles.
The metro line across it was suspended for a while, although by mid-afternoon it had been restored. The mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said road transport in one direction was also being partially restored.
On the Pivnichnyi bridge, a man with a bag of tennis rackets on his back was gazing at the crater in front of him. He was heading home from the courts after he had travelled on foot to the left bank.
"It is upsetting," Anatolii told us. "Then when you read the news of what our side did to the Crimea bridge, you do feel a bit better."
That is because there was a battle of the bridges overnight.
Ukrainian missiles hit the one Russia had built to occupied Crimea, and caused serious damage. That bridge is prized by Russian President Vladimir Putin personally, a symbol of his illegal 2014 takeover.
Ukrainians loathe it for the same reason and now a section has collapsed into the sea, along with its towering arch.
To many here, the timing feels significant: a blow to Putin's image, just as he wants to seem most powerful at this week's summit with the US and China.
But for Kyiv resident Antonina, today is just another challenge to overcome.
The 67-year-old, who we met pulling a shopping trolley through the debris on a bridge in the Ukrainian capital, was heading to see her son on the right bank, but taxi drivers were charging a fortune to go round, so she decided to walk.
"What else could I do?" she shrugged.
"It was a very scary night. It felt like something exploded right over my head. We will get through this, but I just wish the war would end."

articles.title: Indian woman gang-raped while pregnant in 2002 'heartbroken' after two perpetrators bailed
articles.snippet: Bilkis Bano has spoken of her "pain, shock and disbelief" at the top court order and vowed to fight back.
articles.full_text:
Gujarat riots gang-rape survivor 'heartbroken' after bail for two convicts
- Published
The article has details that some readers may find disturbing
A pregnant Muslim woman who was gang-raped and saw 14 family members murdered during the 2002 Gujarat riots has spoken of her "pain, shock and disbelief" after two of her rapists were recently granted bail.
Bilkis Bano said in a statement that she heard about the top court order through press reports and vowed to fight back.
The freed men are from a group of 11 convicts - part of a Hindu mob - serving life terms for the attack on Bano.
All the men were also freed in 2022 after a Gujarat government order. That decision, and the celebrations as they left prison, caused global outrage. In 2024, the Supreme Court overturned the order.
In a short three-page order dated 28 October, the Supreme Court granted bail to Bipinchand Kanaiyalal Joshi and Pradip Ramanlal Modhiya and suspended their sentences while their petition challenging a 2017 Bombay High Court order is being heard.
The judges explained that the early release was because the two convicts "have been under incarceration for a period of more than 17 years" and "that one of the appellants has a severe handicap".
On Tuesday, Bano's lawyer Shobha Gupta told the BBC that the news of Joshi and Modhiya's release had left "Bilkis heartbroken".
"She has to restart her battle for justice. She had no information that this case was coming up in the Supreme Court. What is troubling for us is that every time something like this happens, we worry that it could affect her faith in judiciary."
Gupta said it was difficult to understand why the convicts were being released because "it's not a routine criminal case, it's a case that shocks the conscience of the world, of entire humanity".
The attack on Bano and her family was one of the most horrific crimes during the Gujarat riots, which began after 60 Hindu pilgrims were killed in a fire on a passenger train in the town of Godhra.
Hindu mobs attacked Muslim neighbourhoods, blaming them for starting the fire. The riots continued for three days and more than 1,000 people died, most of them Muslims.
When rioters attacked Bano's village and started setting Muslim homes on fire, she and 16 relatives went on the run. She was 19, had a three-year-old daughter and was pregnant with her second child.
They were attacked on the morning of 3 March 2002 by a group of men "with swords and sticks", she told me in 2017. Her three-year-old daughter, she said, was snatched from her lap and killed.
Her attackers were her neighbours, men she had seen almost daily while growing up. They tore off her clothes and several of them raped her, ignoring her pleas for mercy.
Her cousin, who had given birth two days earlier, was raped and murdered and her newborn baby was killed too.
Bano survived only because she lost consciousness and her attackers left, believing she was dead. Two boys - seven and four - were the only other survivors of the massacre.
Her fight for justice has been long and nightmarish. The first arrests were made only in 2004 after the Supreme Court called in federal investigators and transferred her case to Mumbai, saying that courts in Gujarat could not deliver justice to her.
In her statement released on Monday night, Bano spoke of "fresh tears of pain, shock and disbelief".
"I still cannot believe that once again, for the second time, an order has been passed by the Supreme Court without calling me up and without hearing me," she said.
"For 24 long years, I have stood up to fight for justice... again and again. Yet today, I find myself losing the very justice I had fought so hard to win.... And I am scared of losing faith in justice, yet again."
Bano vowed to "fight this order... for my children, who do not deserve to live haunted by fears and scars for the rest of their lives".
"I do this for my three-year-old Saleha who deserved to live and whose memory demands justice. I do this for women everywhere. Because no woman, no survivor, no citizen should have to endure this eternal test of belonging and equality, and fight for justice for the rest of her life."
Prime Minister Narendra Modi was Gujarat chief minister at the time of the riots, and was criticised for not doing enough to prevent the carnage. He has always denied wrongdoing and has not apologised for the riots.

More than 100,000 take part in France pay protests
Government says 146,000 take part in rallies across France, as CGT trade union put the nationwide total over 500,000.
More than 100,000 people have taken to the streets in France to protest against the high cost of living, with public sector workers demanding pay increases.
The Interior Ministry said on Tuesday that a total of 146,000 people took part in the protests, with 28,000 in Paris alone. The CGT trade union put the nationwide total at just over 500,000 demonstrators.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3Young French students who see ‘no change’ keep up protests in Paris suburbs
- list 2 of 3Why are Europe’s governments struggling to respond to growing protests?
- list 3 of 3France summons Iran’s ambassador over supermarket fridge ‘sabotage’
Several trade unions had called for a day of strike action. Participants included public sector workers, as well as school pupils and university students.
France’s 5.8 million public sector employees were pushed to mobilise after talks with Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu on Friday failed to satisfy union demands. Union representatives left the meeting organised by Lecornu saying the proposed measures failed to address the urgency of the pay situation.
Tuesday’s rally is the third call for a united day of action and strikes in the public sector since September.
Unions have been pushing for across-the-board pay rises since last week’s boost to the minimum wage for private-sector workers.
Protesters say “they simply can’t make ends meet, and they want the government to help them put more money into funding in terms of salaries, in terms of raising the minimum wage”, Al Jazeera’s Natacha Butler reported from Paris.
“The government’s already offered about $30 extra a month on the minimum wage, but those here say that is simply not enough. With inflation, with the way the prices are going up, they say they actually need more.”
The unions put the loss of purchasing power for public servants at 16 percent since 2017, leading to increasing numbers of public employees ending up on or close to the minimum wage against a backdrop of inflation.
“The government doesn’t have much margin or wiggle room financially, because of France’s ballooning debt, and the government’s in the middle of trying to push through a budget with cost-cutting measures in it,” Butler said.
Public-sector workers aim to pressure the government to unfreeze the pay scale point used to calculate their basic salary. However, the government has ruled out any general pay rise for the fourth consecutive year in its draft budget.
“The people in the street know there is only so far you can go; the government knows they do not have a lot of economic wiggle room. Yet nobody really is coming up with another solution,” Butler said.
Despite the government’s efforts to ease tensions, demonstrations have roiled the country for over a month.
Student-led protests demanding better conditions in education erupted in mid-September, but the movement has since expanded in scope to cover a range of issues, from high fuel prices to wages and social housing
Protests for higher wages, lower costs of living and better public services have also spread across Europe.

articles.title: NSA Net, agency’s classified internal network, faces unspecified disruptions

articles.snippet: The NSA has ordered staggered arrivals at its headquarters at Fort Meade, Maryland, as technicians work to fully restore the classified internal network NSA Net.
articles.full_text:
NSA Net, agency’s classified internal network, faces unspecified disruptions
Editor's Note: Story updated 2:30 Eastern U.S. time with statement from the NSA.
The National Security Agency’s classified internal communications network is experiencing what is believed to be a technical issue, resulting in a delayed opening and staggered employee arrivals.
The difficulties with the system, known as NSA Net, are not believed to be the result of a cyberattack, according to two people familiar with the ongoing situation. CNN first reported the development.
NSA “experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance. While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues,” an agency spokesman said in a statement.
The organization’s “infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events."
There was a staggered arrival at agency headquarters, located at Fort Meade, Maryland, specifically because officials want to reduce the load of tens of thousands of personnel signing in the morning at the same time on the same network, one source told Recorded Future News.
This same person noted that the system is not completely shut down, but is only providing intermittent service.
Another person said NSA Net has been unstable for weeks, prompting frustration among employees.
NSA backup centers located around the country are expected to pick up the slack caused by the delay and conduct the agency’s chief mission of collecting signals intelligence from around the globe.
The disturbance at the secretive spy agency is the latest in a series of high-profile technical disruptions that have impacted the United States in recent days — though there is no evidence that they are linked.
Last week there was a day-long, global outage that crippled software produced by tech giant Microsoft, including Outlook. On Monday, a senior company official revealed a months-old bug was responsible for the blackout, which lasted for 24 hours and lingered through the weekend.
On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a nationwide ground stop that halted all U.S. departing flights for more than four hours. The agency has since traced the issue to a single router in Arkansas.
Still, the FBI on Tuesday said its cybersecurity teams are working with the FAA, the Transportation Department and contractor L3Harris “providing technical assistance following Friday’s air traffic communications outage.”
The NSA has experienced glitches in the past, including in 2013 when its public website went dark. Though some hackers claimed they had crashed the site with a denial of service attack, officials said it was the result of a scheduled update.
In 2000, the agency’s computers went dark for three days. The issues were eventually attributed to a software anomaly and infrastructure problems. Recovery required thousands of man-hours and the agency reportedly spent $1.5 million to restore its IT infrastructure.
Martin Matishak
is the senior cybersecurity reporter for The Record. Prior to joining Recorded Future News in 2021, he spent more than five years at Politico, where he covered digital and national security developments across Capitol Hill, the Pentagon and the U.S. intelligence community. He previously was a reporter at The Hill, National Journal Group and Inside Washington Publishers.
