articles.title: LaNeve formally nominated for Army chief of staff role
articles.snippet: The Trump administration nominated Gen. Christopher LaNeve as chief of staff of the Army.
articles.full_text:
The Trump administration nominated Gen. Christopher LaNeve as chief of staff of the Army, according to a Monday congressional notice, moving formally to fill the role left vacant after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired Gen. Randy George in April.
LaNeve, also the Army’s vice chief of staff, has been serving as the acting chief of staff in the interim. He needs Senate confirmation to officially take the position.
“He is the right leader at the right time to modernize the Army and ensure our soldiers are prepared to dominate on any battlefield. I cannot think of anyone better to serve as our next Chief of Staff of the Army,” Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in a social media statement regarding LaNeve’s nomination. Telle said he anticipated “working with the Senate” to get LaNeve — and Lt. Gen. Marcus Evans, who would take on vice chief responsibilities — confirmed.
The administration nominated Evans to fill the role of vice chief of staff of the Army, according to another Monday congressional notice.
After former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned in September amid reported tension with Hegseth, the Army has been without Senate-confirmed top uniformed and civilian leadership. Telle has not been officially nominated to fill the Army secretary role.
LaNeve, who formerly served as Hegseth’s military aide, was nominated for the vice chief role before former Vice Chief James Mingus had completed the typical four-year term in the position. Hegseth’s tenure in the Pentagon has been marked by senior leadership shakeups and the firing of over a dozen generals and admirals.
LaNeve has drawn congressional ire for eliminating the 600-member “Unmanned Assault Battalion,” which was created as part of the 173rd Airborne Brigade. He has since sought to reassure industry leaders that the Army is committed to autonomy, changing the name of the command charged with shaping the future force to U.S. Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command, or FASCOM.
Evans is currently serving as director of Army staff in Washington, according to the service. Previously, he was special assistant to the commanding general at Fort Shafter, Hawaii. He also worked as the special operations command chief of staff from 2021 to 2023, and commanded the Special Operations Joint Task Force-Afghanistan from 2020 to 2021.
He was promoted lieutenant general in September of last year and major general in February 2022.
The nominations come after massive Republican losses during midterm elections, which will shift control of the House and Senate to Democrats during the next year’s congressional session.

articles.title: Finland’s Iceye bids €2 billion for Italian rocket maker Avio
articles.snippet: Finnish satellite operator Iceye made a €2 billion ($2.2 billion) cash offer for Italian rocket maker Avio on Tuesday, with the goal of creating an integrated European space and defense group.
articles.full_text:
ROME — Finnish operator Iceye has a made €2 billion cash offer ($2.2 billion) for Italian rocket maker Avio which would integrate Europe’s space capabilities as well as putting Iceye in charge of Avio’s expansion into the U.S. missile business.
The proposed deal fits with efforts to reduce reliance on external providers and narrow a widening gap with industry leaders in the U.S. and China.
“Europe’s need for sovereign space and defense capabilities is growing. Building the industrial capacity to meet that demand takes years, which makes it critical to invest now,” said Iceye on Tuesday.
The firm said it would invest €1 billion in Avio in Italy over five years in a bid to expand the customer base of Avio’s Vega rocket.
The Finnish government backed the offer, with Finnish Defense Minister Antti Hakkanen stating, “If completed … a global space industry player will be created, through which the self-sufficient security of supply of Finland’s and all of Europe’s defense will rise to a new level.”
Avio said on Tuesday it was considering the offer, while the CEO of Italian state controlled defense group Leonardo, which owns an 18% percent stake in Avio, said he was “pleasantly surprised” by the bid and would consider it.
Avio’s board held a first meeting on Tuesday and said it had started assessing the bid, which Iceye said offered a 21.3% premium to the Italian group’s closing price on Monday or a 34.8% premium to its three-month volume-weighted average price.
Apart from its European space launch activity, Avio is also a market leader in solid rocket motors for missiles. In September it broke ground in Hurt, Virginia, on a new U..S facility to fulfill an ambition to bring much needed extra capacity to U.S. missile production.
Avio has already partnered with Raytheon on production of the Mk 104 dual-thrust rocket motor and has teamed with Lockheed Martin to produce motors at Hurt for Lockheed’s Extended Range GMLRS (ER GMLRS) and Precision Strike Missile (PrSM) programs.
An Avio spokesman told Defense News that U.S. government approval would be required in the event of a takeover by Iceye, as well as Italian government approval.
In September, Avio announced a nine month order intake of €237 million, of which half was defense related, with the remainder mainly related to its Vega C and Vega E launchers.
Iceye said its €41-per-share offer will be launched through wholly owned Italian subsidiary Iris 2 with the aim of delisting the company. Avio shares climbed more than 15% to around €39.5 on the news.
Iceye has supplied Ukraine with satellite radar imagery since 2022, and last month signed a letter of intent with Nokia and Ukraine’s Defence Ministry to explore cooperation in space, including sovereign satellite communications.
Speaking at an event in Helsinki, Iceye CEO Rafal Modrzewski said the company had held consultations with the parties involved, including governments, before launching the bid, and that it would take a few more months to close the transaction.
“It’s a phenomenal combination of capabilities … bringing a full vertical integration, following quite clear industry trends,” Modrzewski said, adding that it would be beneficial for both companies.
With material from Reuters by Giulia Segreti and Essi Lehto.

articles.title: Lithuanian president says US troop rotations will continue beyond latest deployment
articles.snippet: Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said that U.S. troop rotations in the country would continue beyond the current nine-month deployment.
articles.full_text:
Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said on Monday that U.S. troop rotations in Lithuania would continue beyond the current nine-month deployment, speaking at a ceremony marking the arrival of the latest two U.S. battalions.
Washington first deployed troops to Lithuania, a NATO member bordering Russia and Belarus, in 2014 after Russia’s annexation of Crimea.
Since 2019, it had maintained an armoured battalion of about 1,000 troops on overlapping rotations until the Pentagon paused it earlier this year pending a force posture review.
At the Pabrade military base near the Belarusian border, Nauseda said: “As far as I know, this is not a one-off or a temporary rotation. There is a certain rotation plan extending into the future.”
The U.S. Embassy in Lithuania did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
U.S. Ambassador Kara McDonald, speaking at the same ceremony, did not directly comment on Nauseda’s remarks but described the deployment as “a continuation of rotations” that have taken place since 2014.
“Our purpose here is very clear,” she told reporters. “It is a defensive purpose to project deterrence, to maintain readiness, to stand shoulder to shoulder with our allies. This very much is peace through strength, and this is how we preserve peace.”
Lithuania has proposed expanding U.S. presence or making it permanent and has offered to cover the costs.
President Donald Trump told reporters last month his administration would “certainly look at” Lithuania’s request.
Lithuania has tripled defense spending since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and is NATO’s biggest defense spender this year by share of gross domestic product at 5.33%.
Germany is due to station a combat-ready army brigade of about 5,000 troops in Lithuania by the end of next year as a deterrent to Russia.

articles.title: Trump seeks nuclear cuts at summit with Putin and Xi, but prospects are low
articles.snippet: From the U.S. side, meanwhile, the Trump administration surprised many observers by pushing for discussions about reducing nuclear weapons while in Shenzhen.
articles.full_text:
VIENNA — The leaders of the U.S., Russia and China are set to meet in the Chinese tech metropolis of Shenzhen on Thursday in an event that has been hailed as “historic” by all sides. Among the topics raised for discussion are reductions in global nuclear stockpiles. But experts caution that while the meeting itself is a positive development, any major breakthrough remains unlikely.
Expectations for the get-together ratcheted up over the course of the past week, particularly in Russia, where the event has been ascribed undertones of a “Yalta 2.0,” referencing the 1945 conference that reordered the world after World War II.
From the U.S. side, meanwhile, the Trump administration surprised many observers by pushing for discussions about reducing nuclear weapons while in Shenzhen. The last strategic arms control treaty between Russia and the U.S., in the form of New START, expired in February, leaving the two largest nuclear states without numerical limits on atomic arsenals for the first time since 1972.
China, meanwhile, was not a party to New START and was, in fact, never part of any strategic arms treaty like it. Beijing is estimated to have the third-largest nuclear arsenal in the world, at several hundred, although analysts believe it has been working to significantly increase this number in recent years. The U.S. and Russia each have stockpiles of around 4,000 nuclear weapons.
This numerical discrepancy is also why China has previously bristled at the idea of discussing strategic arms limitation in a trilateral format like the one U.S. President Donald Trump has been pushing in the run-up to the meeting. Although Beijing has confirmed the meeting, it has stopped short of officially saying strategic arms dialogue would be on the agenda. “The three presidents will have an in-depth exchange of views on safeguarding world peace and enabling strategic stability in major-country relations,” said Mao Ning, spokesperson for the Chinese Foreign Ministry.
This avoids naming explicitly what the U.S. has asked for. “The President has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous,” White House spokesperson Olivia Wales told reporters last Friday.
Nikita Degtyarev, research coordinator at the Vienna-based Open Nuclear Network, an international NGO dealing with nuclear arms control, said he was realistic about achievable outcomes.
“I don’t have very high expectations, but I’m happy that it’s happening,” he said in an interview. “A meeting at the leader level is something else than the ongoing P5 dialogue and other existing formats.”
The P5 dialogue brings together the five Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty-recognized nuclear weapons states – the U.S., Russia, China, France and the U.K. – on a working level to discuss nuclear policy and risk reduction.
“If there is any outcome of the trilateral meeting relating to nuclear issues, it will likely be more of a political statement than a verifiable and restrictive arms control agreement,” said Heather Williams, director of the Project on Nuclear Issues and senior fellow at the Washington-based think tank CSIS,
“I think the most likely significant outcome would be a reiteration of the Reagan-Gorbachev mantra that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought,” Degtyarev said. A more substantive or groundbreaking agreement was also unlikely because there simply wasn’t enough time for lower-level officials to hammer out the details of any possible agreement that the leaders could sign, he said.
Major arms control treaties often take years of meticulous crafting at the working level before heads of state come together to sign them.
Trump first raised the topic of denuclearization in the context of the summit to reporters on Oct. 19, a day after the Wall Street Journal first reported about a proposed trilateral meeting.
A possible wildcard agenda item remains in the form of artificial intelligence in nuclear weapons. AI in nuclear command and control has emerged as a somewhat more promising topic and a potential area for agreement more palatable to all sides than commitments to numerical reductions or verification mechanisms.
The South China Morning Post reported Nov. 11, citing sources familiar with preparations, that working-level teams had discussed AI in critical weapons systems and that the agenda was shifting toward potential common ground, particularly AI’s role in nuclear command and control. One source characterized AI governance of nuclear weapons as an “easy deliverable” consistent with past policies.
This “could give Trump something to announce without requiring anyone to compromise their nuclear posture,” Lizzi Lee, a fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute, told the French press agency AFP.
Under the previous U.S. administration, Biden and Xi reaffirmed the importance of human decision-making in nuclear command and control in November 2024, while Russia has so far resisted such language, including in the P5 process.
Much may depend on the willingness of Beijing to engage in strategic arms dialogue, which has indicated it has no major desire to discuss this topic while China remains a numerical underdog in the quantity of its warheads.
“China is the host and will probably closely stage-manage the event and the agenda,” Degtyarev said. Xi Jinping’s style of international engagements tends to be highly scripted and predictable, at odds with Trump’s more improvisational approach.
The common denominator for all three leaders is more likely to be good publicity. “Trump is probably genuine about his interest in nuclear arms reduction,” Degtyarev assessed, “but probably also from a self-serving and PR point of view.”
Though the meeting is historic in nature for its assembling of a triumvirate of the world’s most powerful men, “the Yalta 2.0 comparisons are overblown,” said Degtyarev. “The scale of the historical moment is simply different.”

articles.title: Pentagon fails ninth straight audit despite progress in organizing finances
articles.snippet: The Pentagon failed a financial audit for the ninth consecutive year, according to an inspector general report, but an official said a majority of its units passed for the first time.
articles.full_text:
The Pentagon failed a financial audit for the ninth consecutive year, according to an inspector general report released Monday, but an official said a majority of its units passed for the first time.
Defense Department CFO Jules Hurst told Reuters an independent auditor found that financial statements for 14 of the Pentagon’s 25 standalone reporting entities passed in the 2026 fiscal year, which ended in September, up from 11 the prior year. Those entities account for 56% of the department’s assets and 86% of its liabilities.
“For the first time ever, a majority of assets from the department are on clean opinions,” Hurst said. The audits check whether financial statements are fairly presented and whether financial systems and processes are sound.
The Pentagon is a vast bureaucracy that has struggled with some 149 financial management systems, many of which are inadequate and outdated. They include technology built on 50-year-old computer code.
As the administration seeks a record $1.5 trillion in national defense spending from Congress, modernizing those systems has become a priority as the Pentagon strives to show lawmakers it can be trusted.
The Pentagon as a whole was first audited in 2018 and has consistently failed to pass annual audits because of its system and accounting problems. Congress gave it 10 years to pass, which falls in the fiscal year starting in October 2027.
Among the entities passing an audit for the first time in fiscal 2026 was the Pentagon’s Medicare-Eligible Retiree Health Care Fund.
To complete an audit without relying on the antiquated systems, officials drew from 61 core systems in the Pentagon’s more modern cloud-based War Data Platform. They obtained statistically significant data samples that were used for the audit.
The department is also using artificial intelligence tools from Palantir and xAI, alongside in-house applications, to automate financial reconciliations and documentation.
“Passing the audit is ultimately a time problem,” Hurst said, saying AI allows auditors to test more data.
Beginning this year, the Pentagon plans to consolidate 25 separate audit opinions into eight, ahead of seeking a full department-wide opinion in fiscal 2028.
Congress phased in audit requirements for federal agencies over decades, and most major agencies must have their financial statements audited annually.

articles.title: New pact positions the Philippines as a defense hub for Australian troops
articles.snippet: Top officials from Australia and the Philippines have inked a defense pact to accelerate military coordination, paving the way for rotational troop deployment and Australian investments in Philippine military infrastructure.
articles.full_text:
MANILA, Philippines — Top officials from Australia and the Philippines have inked a defense pact to accelerate military coordination, paving the way for rotational troop deployment and Australian investments in Philippine military infrastructure.
The Nov. 15 Defense Cooperation Agreement, or DCA, is designed to cut administrative bottlenecks and create a more efficient coordination system to fast-track bilateral defense activities.
So far the two countries’ military exchanges have largely fallen under a 1995 memorandum of agreement, while troop exchanges were guided by the Status of Visiting Forces Agreement, signed in 2007 and effective since 2012.
According to Australia’s Department of Defence, the new pact covers intelligence-sharing, military training, the transfer of aerial and surface drones, maritime activities, and military infrastructure.
“This new Defence Cooperation Arrangement will deepen practical cooperation between our defense forces and create new opportunities to work together in support of regional security,” Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said in a statement.
Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. said the new DCA reduces bureaucratic barriers, particularly in troop deployment, and would allow Australia to rapidly deploy troops to aid in Philippine disaster response.
“Rather than 100 steps to do a single thing, it will just now take 10 … and it will be more purposeful and not ad hoc,” Teodoro told reporters following the signing.
The move comes as Australia recalibrates its defense posture in response to China’s expanding military capabilities, growing missile reach, and increasing use of gray-zone tactics and economic coercion in the Indo-Pacific.
“From Australia’s point of view, the Philippines is our first line of defense,” Australian Strategic Policy Institute senior fellow Euan Graham told Defense News.
Australia has experienced harassment by PLA forces, including dangerous maritime maneuvers, laser targeting in its northern exclusive economic zone, and the use of sonar and flares in close proximity to Royal Australian Navy vessels.
Like Australia, the Philippines faces Chinese pressure head-on. Chinese ships have used high-powered water cannons, pointed military-grade lasers, rammed, and attacked Armed Forces of the Philippines vessels and personnel.
When asked if the DCA was meant to boost deterrence in the Taiwan Strait, Teodoro emphasized the agreement will bolster “deterrence in the West Philippine Sea” and in “Philippine territory.”
Strategy shift
Australia marked a historic peacetime shift toward a strategy of denial in 2023, most recently codified in the 2026 national defense strategy.
The idea is to reshape the Australian Defense Force into an integrated, focused military capable of deterring and denying access to its northern approaches, which includes deploying a forward-defense force.
Earlier this year, Australia created the new Littoral Maneuver Group under the 18th Sustainment Brigade headquartered in Brisbane, to operate farther north, making the Philippines an important part of that strategy.
But Australia can only deploy small units, analyst Graham cautioned. And keeping these mobile forces supplied and operational in archipelagic countries like the Philippines is challenging, as troops and equipment are moved across widely dispersed islands during operations.
Building logistics networks
To that end, the new cooperation agreement is expected to facilitate discussions on potential Australian investments in Philippine military infrastructure.
A list of five Luzon bases slated to receive funding for eight infrastructure projects was expected to be finalized around August this year. However, only one base has been discussed in detail so far, officials told Defense News.
Teodoro previously clarified that base agreements with Australia will follow a different model than the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA) between the Philippines and the United States, which includes provisions for prepositioning military equipment and assets.
The Australian “basing” arrangements, officials said, would include areas that are not traditional bases.
Rather than a large basing presence, what the Australian military needs is access to locations that could sustain its forces during operations and contingencies.
Discussions so far have included sustainment and logistics to support joint operations while troops spread across the archipelago’s most complex, most challenging, and remote terrains.
Graham said Australia’s role in the Philippines is distinct but complementary to that of the United States. While physical locations could overlap, the infrastructure projects would be different.
Canberra and Manila in 2021 signed the Mutual Support Logistics Arrangement, which covers fuel and other supplies for aircraft and vessels, transportation, logistics, and coordination.
“The importance of logistics can’t be underestimated. It’s not just about getting your fighting force fighting. You’ve got to supply them with food, fuel, and ammunition during all of that,” Graham said.
More complex training
With the new DCA with Australia in place, joint exercises, especially Exercise ALON, will see a larger iteration next year, Teodoro said.
Exercise ALON, first held in 2023, is the biennial flagship joint training exercise between countries, focused on amphibious operations.
The 2025 edition saw Australia’s largest overseas military exercise for the year and showcased the ADF projecting combat forces into the contested West Philippine Sea, Graham said.
Apart from maritime training, Teodoro said there will be more aerial, land, cyber, and multidomain training exercises between Filipino and Australian troops.
Military officials told Defense News that Army training has been a priority area for the Australian military’s training playbook in the Philippines. The focus follows sweeping changes in both countries’ land forces to prepare them for modern conflicts.
While the Philippine Army expands from its signature jungle and urban warfare expertise toward coastal defense, the Australian ground service has pivoted toward littoral warfare.
Since 2023, exchanges have focused on techniques, tactics, and procedures for amphibious operations, Army spokesperson Col. Louie Dema-ala told Defense News.
But future iterations will include advanced training, Dema-ala said. “We are transitioning into a multi-domain capable Army.”
The exchange is not one-sided. Australia also stands to benefit from the Philippine Army’s experience operating in dense jungle terrain.
“This is not just a one-way process. We can learn from the jungle warfare fighting skills, and I think that’s important to stress. No one can tell us about the Philippines better than the Filipinos,” Graham said.

articles.title: French troops operating in non-combat roles in Ukraine, broadcaster RFI reports
articles.snippet: The troops are part of a structure called Volia, after a Ukrainian word that can be translated as “will” or “freedom,” the French state-owned international news radio said on Monday.
articles.full_text:
PARIS — French troops have been operating in Ukraine in non-combat roles since at least the summer of 2026 to maintain equipment used by the Ukrainian armed forces and provide training, Radio France Internationale reported, citing several unidentified sources familiar with the deployment.
The troops are part of a structure called Volia, after a Ukrainian word that can be translated as “will” or “freedom,” the French state-owned international news radio said on Monday. Volia is headed by a French general, and French troops operating in Ukraine are deployed under the guise of the Gerfaut mission in Poland to train Ukrainian soldiers, RFI said.
France has supplied Ukraine with equipment including Caesar howitzers, Mirage 2000 jets and precision missiles, for which maintenance expertise is being provided by personnel from various French support regiments, according to RFI. The radio broadcaster said it’s not disclosing the names of regiments involved to ensure the safety of soldiers and those around them.
The United Kingdom has also reportedly deployed troops in Ukraine in non-combat roles. Two serving members of the British armed forces are known to have died in the country since Russia’s 2022 invasion, with the U.K. Ministry of Defence confirming both deaths as non-combat accidents away from the front lines.
The structure of Volia is “light and modular,” composed of small teams for short-term missions, and Volia is not a combat mission, according to RFI. France decided against sending civilian technicians because Ukraine is at war, the radio broadcaster said.
While France’s constitution requires the government inform parliament of a conventional force deployment outside the national territory, neither the National Assembly nor the Senate have been informed of the existence of Volia, RFI reported.
Meanwhile, TV broadcaster France Télévisions similarly reported on Monday that France has secretly deployed several dozens of military in Ukraine as part of Volia. The outlet said it had confirmed the RFI information, but it did not disclose how.

articles.title: First permanently assigned F-15EXs touch down at Kadena Air Base
articles.snippet: Kadena Air Base received their first permanently assigned F-15EX Eagle IIs, becoming the first installation abroad and second Air Force location to field the jet.
articles.full_text:
A Japan air base became the first American installation abroad to receive two permanently assigned F-15EX Eagle IIs and the second-ever Air Force location to field the fighter jet.
Kadena Air Base, located in Okinawa, Japan, received two of the fighter aircraft Sunday as the Air Force strives to increase U.S. airpower in the Pacific, according to a recent service release, especially as the base continues to replace its F-15C/D fleet.
“[F-15EXs] strengthen our ability to deter aggression, respond to emerging threats and defend Japan alongside our allies and partners,” 18th Wing Commander Brig. Gen. John Gallemore said in the release.
“Their permanent presence at Kadena reinforces our commitment to the U.S.-Japan alliance and ensures we continue to bring advanced combat capabilities to one of the most strategically important regions in the world,” he continued.
In November 2022, the base first began withdrawing its legacy F-15C/D aircraft after four decades of service. The transition included rotational deployments of fourth- and fifth-generation fighters to maintain a fighter presence while maintainers, operators and mission support airmen sought the expertise needed to utilize a new platform as soon as it reaches operational capability, the release says.
Two years after the Oregon Air National Guard received theirs, the F-15EXs at Kadena are expected to increase the base’s ability to conduct counterair operations and boost the service’s forward-deployed capabilities.
With advanced avionics, modernized electronic warfare systems and heightened weapons-carrying capacity, the aircraft are meant to support bilateral readiness alongside the Japan Air Self-Defense Force and other regional partners.
Kadena’s 44th and 67th Fighter Squadrons are both slated to operate the F-15EXs.
In preparation for the jets’ arrival, operators from the 67th Fighter Squadron, which is part of Kadena’s 18th Operations Group, traveled to Eglin Air Force Base, Florida, and Portland Air National Guard Base, Oregon, to conduct aircraft qualification training.
Personnel from the 18th Aircraft Maintenance Squadron also coordinated with Boeing, the jet’s manufacturer, and teams at Eglin and Portland to progress technical proficiency. The personnel also supported F-15E operations at Seymour-Johnson Air Force Base, North Carolina, and Mountain Home Air Force Base, Idaho, to “keep their skills sharp.”
The news of the fighter’s arrival comes roughly seven months after the Air Force revealed their new acquisition goal regarding the F-15EX Eagle IIs as part of the service’s fiscal 2027 budget request, aiming to more than double the fleet to 267 aircraft, an increase from the previously planned 129 jets.
More recently, the Air Force awarded Boeing a $2.38 billion contract to produce 22 F-15EX Eagle II aircraft, bringing the total number of aircraft to be manufactured by the defense company to 120 under Lots 1 through 7.

articles.title: Biodata, AI and the future of command: Getting it right
articles.snippet: Fitness trackers and AI diagnostics are here to stay. They can provide valuable data for operational planning — if security and privacy are handled properly.
articles.full_text:
As AI and biotech converge, the central question is no longer simply whether the military can collect biological data. The question is how.
Who controls collection? Under what conditions may the data be transmitted? Who is permitted to interpret them? What authority should those interpreters carry in command decisions? I contend that the Pentagon — and, in the last resort, Congress — must govern biodata as an emerging factor in not just military medicine, but in command decisions. Its confidentiality, integrity, availability and operational use are increasingly matters of force protection and command responsibility.
Emerging technologies can collect and interpret indicators of fatigue, cognitive overload, physiological stress, environmental exposure and recovery. The underlying data may include heart rate and variability, sleep and recovery measures, body temperature, blood chemistry, biomarkers of injury or infection and indicators of physiological stress, as well as less obviously medical metrics like movement and activity patterns.
Used responsibly, these capabilities could help commanders anticipate declining endurance, manage force rotations, prioritize limited medical resources and make better-informed decisions about operational readiness. But the same information, in the wrong hands or just mishandled, can expose a unit’s vulnerabilities or distort the decisions on which its mission depends.
There is a critical distinction to make here between raw data and what is done with it, by whom. A sensor measures something; an AI system interprets what that measurement may mean; a commander decides whether that assessment matters to a particular mission. These are different functions, carrying different standards of reliability and responsibility. A heart-rate measurement is not a diagnosis. A sleep deficit is not a complete measure of judgment. A model-generated readiness score is not an order, nor should it become one by default. Human judgment remains essential and humans must be held accountable for their judgments — or for their blind deference to a machine.
So how can the military use biodata right? To start with, during training, biodata could help identify accumulated fatigue, optimize recovery schedules, evaluate exposure to environmental hazards and support earlier medical assessment. Longitudinal data collected over months and years can establish an individual’s baseline, allowing clinicians to assess deviations from that person’s individual range, rather than compare every service member against an undifferentiated population average. Such uses can improve health, training design and force preservation before a deployment begins.
Moving beyond individual health, AI could identify changes in performance across a unit, help anticipate demand for medical services, or inform decisions about when a unit needs to rest and when it can keep operating. When fused with other, more traditional military data — like personnel availability, ammunition stocks, equipment status, intelligence and mission requirements — biodata becomes part of the commander’s broader operational picture.
That increases both the utility and the risk. Medical information becomes command information when an inference about the body begins to influence where, when and how a person or formation is employed. At that point, the military must be able to distinguish legitimate operational awareness from inappropriate surveillance, and decision support from human judgment blindly bowing to a statistical estimate.
Security And Privacy
Before a commander asks what a wearable device can reveal about personnel, a more basic question must be answered: Should that device be active in this environment at all?
In 2018, the Defense Department restricted geolocation capabilities in designated operational areas, recognizing that fitness trackers and related devices could expose personnel locations, routines and force concentrations.
Even data collected during peacetime can create a security risk. Over time, measurements may reveal who trains together, how long units take to recover, how long personnel remain at a facility and when readiness appears to deteriorate. A persistent record of routine behavior can become a map of future military capability — for our own planning or, if leaked, for an adversary’s.
Precisely because biodata is operationally useful, it is also worth stealing or manipulating. An adversary able to access physiological, behavioral and performance data could identify training cycles, recovery windows, deployment patterns, or possible gaps in unit endurance. Or, instead of just stealing biodata, an adversary could alter it, making a capable formation appear unfit for operations or portraying an exhausted unit as ready, which could gaslight commanders to push tired personnel beyond their limits or prematurely withdraw high-functioning forces.
Even security measures can be revealing: If everyone in a given unit turns off their trackers at once, that itself is a signal they’re likely about to be deployed. Restrictions on devices must cover the entire life cycle of the data, not simply the moment of contact.
In short, a personal health tracker may have implications well beyond its individual user — and simply turning off location sharing, or setting a device on “airplane mode,” does not necessarily eliminate the risk.
So the question for commanders is not simply whether a device is approved for purchase or useful during training. It is who has authority to permit, forbid, or restrict the device when security conditions change. A tracker that is valuable during a rehabilitation program or garrison training may be unacceptable near a sensitive installation, during preparations for deployment, or in a conflict zone. Permissions should be specific to the mission and environment, with explicit distinctions between collecting data locally, transmitting it wirelessly, and uploading it to cloud services. In some settings, the correct command decision will be to leave the device behind.
When Medical Information Becomes Command Authority
A second set of questions concerns permissions, identifiability and interpretation: Who can do what, when? Can medical professionals, military superiors and the service members themselves all see the same information? May a commander access an individual’s clinical indicators, or only an operationally relevant summary? Who may share, retain, challenge, or delete a record?
These distinctions must be designed into the policy and the technology, not tacked on ad hoc. Medical staff may need a servicemember’s personal, identifiable information for diagnosis and treatment. A commander may only need a bounded assessment of mission-relevant limitations like fatigue or illness, without access to a full medical history. The individual should have a way to understand how their information is used —and to contest misuse.
Baseline comparisons create another challenge. Comparing a service member with their own validated baseline may be more informative than measuring them against generalized averages across large populations. But illness, local environments, new equipment and incomplete measurements can alter what counts as “normal.” Rather than rubberstamp assessments they don’t understand, commanders should know whether any given assessment reflects a direct measurement, a deviation from an individual baseline, a population-based inference, or an AI-generated prediction and whether the model has been validated for the mission at hand.
AI can illuminate aspects of the problem, but it cannot by itself settle questions of unit cohesion, tactical adaptability, or military necessity. Users must guard against “automation bias,” where humans defer uncritically to computer outputs as if to an oracle, and “metric fixation,” where the ability to measure a few factors leads to ignoring important intangibles. Biological measurements should inform, not silently substitute for, professional military judgment and clinical expertise.
An AI-generated finding can appear more precise than the underlying evidence actually is. Consider a dashboard reporting that a service member is “90 percent ready.” Ready for what task, for how long, under what environmental conditions and according to which validated criteria? A numerical score may compress complex uncertainties into an illusion of simplistic certainty.
Assessments should therefore distinguish between actual measurements, diagnoses based on that hard data and predictions based on those diagnoses, with clear caveats about the uncertainty and limits inherent in any mathematical model. They should also permit a human to challenge and correct potential errors. A clinical judgment, a service member’s report, or a commander’s direct observation may reveal conditions that the model did not capture.
Recommendations: Securing the Biodata Architecture
Overall, a coherent approach to biodata should treat the following factors, not as afterthoughts, but as central to the design of the system:
First, data collection and emissions control must be explicit command decisions. Establish mission-specific rules, designate the authority to issue exceptions and require documented risk assessments for sensitive operations or locations. Build the system to degrade gracefully instead of collapsing as soon as an enemy disrupts the network. Never assume that equipment suitable for peacetime training is suitable for operational deployment.
Second, protect biodata for both individual privacy and operational security. Apply safeguards proportionate to the mission context and the value an adversary could derive from aggregation and correlation with other data. Secure the data pathway end-to-end, starting with vetted sensors and ending with strict rules for long-term retention or storage.
Third, separate clinical access from command use. Establish clear and different levels of access for medical personnel, commanders, analysts and service members. Military leaders should receive the minimum personal information necessary for legitimate decisions, while clinical determinations remain with medical professionals. Specify who may activate monitoring systems, inspect identifiable records, approve secondary uses and audit access.
Fourth, guard against blind trust in algorithmic claims. Require outputs to distinguish individual baselines from population norms, direct observations from predictions and validated results from uncertain inferences. Build in procedures for challenging a score, documenting overrides, correcting errors and preventing unjustified decisions based on incomplete data.
Fifth, assign accountability before operational adoption. Identify who approves new technologies, sets performance thresholds, adjudicates conflicting assessments, reviews risks and investigates failures. Responsibility must remain traceable to identifiable, individual humans.
Finally, train for biodata denial, deception and manipulation. In wargames, present commanders with seemingly credible readiness estimates that conflict with what their medical team, their subordinates, or their own eyes are telling them. Scenarios should include personal trackers transmitting during an exercise, improperly anonymized records exposing a small unit, or an AI tool producing corrupted conclusions. The objective is to develop judgment about when to trust an assessment, when to question it and when to operate without it.
The United States has an opportunity to use AI and biotechnology to strengthen medical care, personnel readiness and military effectiveness. Realizing that potential requires more than deploying sensors or buying analytics. It requires institutions capable of governing when information is created, where it flows, who can interpret it and how much authority it should have over consequential decisions.
Protecting both individual warfighters and the force as a whole requires protecting both the information drawn from the human body and human authority over how it is used. Biodata security is not simply a privacy issue or a medical-technology problem. It is a requirement of force protection, operational resilience and leadership.
Dr. Elise G. Annett is a Research Fellow in the Program for Disruptive Technology and Future Warfare at the Institute for National Strategic Studies, National Defense University, and a Senior Digital Domain Fellow at the Center for the Application of Grand Strategy.
The views and opinions presented in this essay are those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of the United States government, the Department of War, or the National Defense University.

articles.title: NATO kicks off 11-nation Starlift satellite launch program
articles.snippet: Notably, four countries that were original participants of the space effort were left out of today’s announcement — France, Hungary, Luxembourg and the United States.
articles.full_text:
BELFAST — NATO has begun implementing the multinational Starlift space project, which aims to secure military satellite launch services, the alliance said today.
The alliance shared that 10 members (Belgium, Canada, Finland, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, Turkey, and the United Kingdom), alongside South Korea, committed to funding the program through the NATO Support and Procurement Agency (NSPA). The agreement came on the sidelines of a meeting of NATO’s National Armaments Directors at the end of October, according to today’s statement.
First announced in 2024, NATO stresses that Starlift “aims to help participating countries work with commercial launch providers and spaceports to make access to space more resilient, responsive and cost-effective.”
Additionally, the initiative is set to support armed forces with a launch service that will assist with securing slots on commercial rockets, structured around flight from a series of spaceports across NATO territory and South Korea.
The statement did not disclose program costs or partner nations’ financial contributions. Notably, four countries that were original participants of Starlift were left out of today’s announcement — France, Hungary, Luxembourg and the United States. The statement did not share the reason for those nations being left off the statement, but in comments shared with Breaking Defense after publication, a NATO official said the US is taking part as an associated member.
“In this role, it contributes expertise and lessons learned from U.S. initiatives,” added the official. “Given U.S. leadership in the launch sector, this input helps inform STARLIFT’s development, including efforts to promote interoperability.”
More allies and additional partners are expected to join the effort in the future, according to the official.
Other core parts of the program include a forum for developing and testing responsive space operations, such as urgent satellite launches and a plan to improve launch logistics through experimentation.
Europe has a number of launch sites at its disposal, including Norway’s Andøya Spaceport and the UK’s Spaceport, Cornwall. South Korea is studying the construction of a second launch site to expand local capabilities and reduce dependence on foreign services, according to Aviation Week.
UPDATED 11/17/2026 at 1:11 p.m. ET with comment from NATO.

articles.title: Friend or foe becomes the question as skies fill with potential adversaries
articles.snippet: [Sponsored] Quickly and accurately identifying friendly forces requires IFF attuned to drones.
articles.full_text:
Identification Friend or Foe (IFF) technology has been around for decades, but as threats and platforms rapidly evolve, IFF must be adaptable to distinguish allied forces from potential threats and operate in contested and denied environments.
Breaking Defense spoke with Seth Guanu, Combat Identification Products program area director at BAE Systems, about how IFF technology is changing, how it can be used across both U.S. and allied forces, and how it must adapt to meet future threats.
Breaking Defense: IFF technology has been around for a long time. How is it critical to joint forces operations today?
Guanu: IFF is a question-and-answer system. It uses a waveform, which is electrical energy, to transmit data. If you’re a platform and you’re unsure of another platform’s friend status, you ask a question – which is called an interrogation – and the unknown platform responds via secure communications to positively identify itself. Interrogators ask the question, transponders answer the question, and combined interrogator transponders do both. We have these systems on aircraft, ships, land, and radar platforms.
When you look back on history, the introduction of radar was revolutionary. However, radar only showed that something was out there, not whether it was friendly. There needed to be some way of identifying friendly forces where you weren’t spoofed by the enemy. IFF was introduced in World War II and continues to be a critical system.
IFF works alongside radars, data links, sensors and many other systems. For instance, if an adversary attempts to attack our assets from the air, IFF allows our defensive measures to engage threats without endangering friendly forces.
Since that time, warfare has expanded into multiple domains, not only land and sea and air, but space and cyber. Today’s adversaries are more agile and with new technology the speed of conflict has increased dramatically.
When you bring in unmanned systems and associated swarms it adds further complexity beyond what our forces have had to deal with in the past. The Department of War’s Joint All Domain Command and Control strategy (JADC2) strategy helps manage this by connecting assets across domains.
IFF underpins the C2 part of the strategy. This allows joint forces to sense and make sense of data. Is it friend or foe? Then you need to act. You need to be able to do that in split seconds, or you’re not ahead of the adversaries.
With changing threats, such as the proliferation of drones, how is IFF evolving to meet that challenge?
Modern warfare demands technological advances including enhanced cryptology, faster processing, and detection at greater ranges. IFF must be easily upgradeable to meet future threats.
Migrating to software-based IFF skills and card-based solutions is key to providing agility. Our IFF systems use a modular design and open system architecture that allows new capabilities to be integrated through software updates rather than hardware changes. This reduces obsolescence and accelerates enhancements without modifying fleet infrastructure.
Additionally, as unmanned air systems (UAS) expand in threat environments, new technologies are needed to equip the platforms that don’t overload the already crowded IFF frequency band. We are developing this technology and working with the IFF community to define enhancements to Mode 5 to address these changes to the combat environment.
How can IFF be used across both U.S. and allied forces? What are the challenges to ensuring that IFF is being used effectively across joint forces and across all domains?
If you look at IFF or at these missions, say across the U.S. and its coalition, what are the things that you want? You want interoperability and standardization for U.S. and allied operations. Mode 5, the latest secure IFF waveform, is a NATO standard and supports worldwide interoperability.
The challenges associated with ensuring the effective use of Mode 5 across joint forces come from the significant number of different nations, platforms and manufacturers deploying unique IFF systems. In the U.S., the Air Traffic Control Radar Beacon System (ATCRBS), Identification Friend or Foe (IFF), and Mark XII Systems (AIMS) office ensures compatibility across U.S. and NATO forces.
Certifying equipment at both the box level and platform level is critical to overall system performance. The recent AIMS box-level certification of our AN/APX-127(V)1 Combined Interrogator Transponder is a major milestone. The new CIT provides advanced, multi-function capabilities while supporting the latest crypto and cybersecurity resilience requirements. The AIMS certification means the product is ready for use and can serve as a drop-in replacement for current systems.
In addition to having the same tools and waveform, everyone must operate under a consistent concept of operations (CONOPS), otherwise interoperability breaks down and then challenges can occur.
What are the benefits of a combined system and how does it differ from a standalone interrogator or transponder?
Ships typically use interrogators as a key element of their combat ID system to identify airborne objects while aircraft generally carry transponders to respond to questions.
A combined interrogator transponder (CIT) provides both capabilities in one box. This is essential for tactical aircraft that need to engage and where space for equipment is limited on the platform.
By combining both functions, CITs reduce size, weight and power demands and require only a single supporting infrastructure. Whether a platform uses an interrogator, transponder, or both depends on the mission and CONOPS.
How do you work around concerns about things such as jamming and spoofing?
IFF is a radio frequency (RF)-based solution, which can be subject to electronic warfare (EW) attacks. There’s constant evolution with RF so staying ahead of threats is crucial.
We are one of the key co-architects of the secure Mode 5 waveform, and our systems employ anti-jam techniques to operate in this contested environment.
We’re constantly maturing our technology, to support the latest crypto, anti-jam and cybersecurity resilient requirements. At a recent AIMS User Working Group, we successfully demonstrated our latest transponder’s resilience by introducing live RF jamming during the demo.
How long has BAE Systems been involved with IFF? What are your key areas of focus in IFF as you look forward?
BAE Systems has more than 80 years of IFF experience. Since Mode 5’s introduction in the mid-2000s, we have delivered more than 1,500 interrogators, 6,000 combined interrogator-transponder systems and 16,000 transponders across 140 platform types in more than 40 countries. Our systems support U.S. and coalition forces and air defense, weapons systems, air traffic control, and range instrumentation.
We develop solutions to outpace modern threats. We’ve seen a huge improvement in capability driving advanced performance while reducing size, weight and power. Modular firmware and software-defined architectures enable upgrades and integration into next-generation platforms.
Adversaries are agile so we must be faster by anticipating threats, developing counter technology and fielding updates quickly. Our next-generation products are designed as drop-in upgrades. With robust hardware processing capability, we can constantly update firmware and software after deployment to provide a new capability to address new threats.
Our enhancements, such as anti-jam and cyber resilience features, continue to lead in the industry. We’re listening to our customers. The future of IFF is a system that’s easily upgradeable, integrated, affordable and effective.
I’m proud to be part of the team at BAE Systems and our mission: “We Protect Those Who Protect Us.” We remain committed to delivering systems that meet today’s requirements and can rapidly adapt to tomorrow’s challenges.

articles.title: Senate appropriators unveil $1.1T Pentagon spending bill, folding in reconciliation priorities
articles.snippet: Nearly $69 billion in money sought by the White House through reconciliation will be rolled into the base budget under the Senate appropriator’s plan.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON – Senate appropriators are proposing nearly $1.1 trillion in defense spending for fiscal 2027, a historic figure that includes key priorities but still falls well short of the $1.5 trillion figure sought by the Trump administration.
Until tonight’s release of a proposed spending plan, the Senate Appropriations defense subcommittee was the last of the four defense committees to put forth a budget offering. Now its $1.1 trillion figure will have to be sorted out with a slightly lower topline from its House counterparts. (The Armed Services Committees in the House and Senate both included a topline $1.14 trillion figure, though it is not directly comparable to that of the appropriations committees.)
The Trump administration’s $1.5 trillion ask was split into two categories: $1.15 trillion in the base budget and $350 billion in a reconciliation bill. So far, lawmakers have not moved out with that reconciliation request that funds big-ticket priorities like Golden Dome, critical munitions and the bulk of a $55 billion push for the new Defense Autonomous Warfare Group (DAWG).
The White House has pushed to still pass that $350 billion by reconciliation, but there has been little sign that will happen. According to Punchbowl News, the top Republican in the Senate, John Thune, declined today to say whether a defense-only reconciliation bill is being actively considered.
RELATED: The fight over the FY27 defense budget is on. Here’s 13 key issues for Congress to resolve.
Senate appropriators are not fans of the reconciliation process, as it takes control of the money out of their hands and gives it to the authorizers. That sentiment was seemingly echoed in a statement from Sen. Mitch McConnell, the defense appropriations subcommittee chair who is retiring at the close of this Congress, who wrote, “This bill is a roadmap to sustainably and responsibly delivering generational investments in the national defense … The nature of warfare is changing, and America’s adversaries are working together to threaten us. Deterring these threats is a project bigger than one-time surges of cash.”
Instead, Senate appropriators are now seeking to funnel some of the Trump priorities into items in their proposal.
“Of this $1.1 trillion, nearly $69 billion, that was initially requested as one-time mandatory spending by the administration, is provided as discretionary funds in order to provide stable, sustainable, and predictable funding for critical capabilities across the Joint Force,” lawmakers wrote in a summary [pdf] of the proposed legislation.
For example, their spending bill includes $9.4 billion for Golden Dome and $3 billion for DAWG; both totals fall far short of the Pentagon’s request, but would be enough keep both initiatives going. The proposed bill includes $47.2 billion to buy munitions with the bulk of the funds, $40.6 billion, directed towards multi-year contracts like Advanced Medium-Range Air to Air Missile, Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement and Precision Strike Missile Increment 1 – key agreements that are in place, in principle, with contractors but have yet to be funded.
Appropriators would also move to rescue other high-priority items like F-35 fighter jets amid dim prospects for a reconciliation bill. Noting that the Trump administration banked on reconciliation to fund 53 jets alongside 32 in its base budget request, appropriators would add roughly half that amount, budgeting an increase of $4.1 billion to buy an additional five conventional takeoff and landing F-35As, five jump-jet F-35Bs and 15 carrier-launched F-35Cs.
Under the SAC’s plan, the Army would see an increase in both procurement and research, development test and evaluation funds, mainly for its aviation programs.
The committee recommended increasing the funding for the Boeing-made Chinook CH-47 helicopters from $210.6 million in the president’s budget to $570.6 million. This is also more than the House committee recommended for the program at $456 million.
The committee also recommended adding $185 million for the Improved Turbine Engine Program which was zeroed out in the president’s budget. The House committee previously recommended $155 million for the program — which aims to field an engine designed to provide a 50 percent increase in horsepower and a 25 percent improved fuel efficiency rate for the service’s Apache and Blackhawk helos.
Regarding counter drone capabilities for the Army, the committee recommended an increase of $150 million for more Coyote Block 2 and Block 3 platforms, but recommended a decrease of $65.6 million for the Enduring-High Energy Laser program, stating it is “ahead of need.”
When it comes to shipbuilding, the Senate panel included $42 billion with $1.9 billion in additional funding for a second DDG 51 destroyer.
To help pay for unforeseen costs, senate appropriators also included $1.7 billion to “mitigate the department’s projected FY2027 fuel shortfall,” along with $1.9 billion in “flexible readiness funding” to address emerging and unfunded requirements.
Next Steps
The Senate spending bill still needs to work its way through the chamber and receive a vote on the floor before Senate and House leaders decide on the next steps for passing a single bill to the president. And Congressional leaders need to sort it all out by Dec. 11, when the continuing resolution funding the government expires; otherwise, they will have to extend the CR or face a government shutdown.
While US President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have continued to publicly push for $1.5 trillion to fund the Pentagon this year, in September the department’s comptroller Jules Hurst told Breaking Defense said he is prepared to work with lawmakers to figure out how to shuffle key priorities.
“If we really want to fund those things, then we have an opportunity to go back to the appropriators before they finalize the bill, at least I think we will…. it’s a conversation, obviously,” Hurst said at the time.
“The question would be, what’s more important to have money for in FY27 [or] can it wait for FY28,” he later added. “And, a lot of these technological areas [are] evolving so fast. Some things we need the money right now to invest in change. … Other things we need to do a little more research and development.”

articles.title: Uber says nearly 150,000 impacted by third-party breach
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: In breach notification letters, the rideshare company said it was notified by a third party service provider on October 9 that internal credentials were stolen and used to access Uber’s account.
articles.full_text:
Uber says nearly 150,000 impacted by third-party breach
Uber warned regulators in multiple states that a recent data breach exposed the names and driver’s licenses of 149,346 people across the U.S.
In breach notification letters, the rideshare company said it was notified by a third party service provider on October 9 that internal credentials were stolen and used to access Uber’s account.
Uber’s investigation into the incident found that the hackers accessed images of driver’s licenses and extracted text data, including names, addresses, dates of birth and driver’s license numbers. The impacted data was in a cloud storage environment created by Uber specifically to enable the service provider’s work.
Uber did not respond to requests for comment about the name of the provider.
Uber said it immediately severed its data connections to the provider once it was notified of the cyberattack and its investigation into the attack is ongoing. The company has since deleted or rotated credentials and access information associated with the service provider.
Uber’s investigation found that the company’s environment was “subject to Uber’s cloud security management processes and overseen by Uber’s Cloud Security team.” But they were not alerted “because the unauthorized third party used valid credentials.”
The compromise of the service provider’s system allowed the hackers to access the data and not trigger any alerts.
“The service provider’s compromised credentials did not provide access to other Uber systems,” Uber added.
Uber is the largest rideshare service in the world, reporting $14.8 billion in revenue last quarter.
TechCrunch, which first reported the breach last week, said the incident is tied to a cyberattack on AI infrastructure company Fireworks. Fireworks warned in an advisory last week that cybercriminals stole billing information and AI-specific data during two breaches last month.
Fireworks said the attacks are part of a larger string of breaches recently spotlighted by incident responders at Google. Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant published a recent blog about a tactic known as "LLMJacking” where hackers hijack an enterprise’s access to large language models.
Mandiant said it has responded to multiple LLMJacking incidents in 2026 spanning a variety of cloud and LLM providers while impacting “organizations in North America, South America, and Asia Pacific across the financial services, retail, technology, and transportation sectors.”
Since Fireworks came forward, customers like Notion and Cursor have warned that they were affected by the incident as well.
Jonathan Greig
is a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

Ride-hailing company Uber is notifying nearly 150,000 drivers that attackers stole their data after breaching AI infrastructure provider Fireworks in early October.
In breach notification letters sent to affected individuals on November 10, Uber said threat actors accessed their personal information after breaching an Uber account with a third-party service provider.
While Uber didn't share the total number of affected drivers in these letters, it revealed in a filing with Maine's Office of the Attorney General that the data breach has exposed the information of 149,346 drivers, including their names, driver’s license numbers, dates of birth, and addresses.
After being informed of the breach, Uber launched an investigation and severed data connections with the service provider to block further malicious access to its data.
"On October 9, 2026, a service provider notified Uber that an unauthorized third party had compromised the service provider's internal credentials and used them to access Uber's account with the service provider," Uber said. "After being notified of this incident, Uber immediately severed data connections with the service provider and launched an investigation. On October 13, 2026, our investigation determined that the unauthorized party had used the compromised credentials to access Uber data connected to the service provider."
Although the company didn't directly name the hacked service provider, TechCrunch first reported that the Uber data breach stems from an October 24 security incident at AI training provider Fireworks, which was hacked after a third-party cloud provider hack.
Fireworks has attributed the attack to a financially motivated cybercriminal threat actor group linked to a series of large language model hijacking (LLMjacking) attacks.
The Fireworks breach also led to security incidents at AI coding platform Cursor and digital workspace platform Notion, which also reported that the attackers stole data from a limited number of customers and (in Cursor's case) infected users' devices with backdoor malware.
An Uber spokesperson was not immediately available for comment when BleepingComputer reached out for more information about the data breach.
The company disclosed another data breach in December 2022 after a threat actor leaked IT asset information, employees' email addresses, and corporate reports stolen from third-party service provider Teqtivity.
Uber previously confirmed that hackers who breached some of its systems in October 2016 stole data from 50 million users and 7 million drivers, and that the Lapsus$ extortion group also hacked it in September 2022 in an MFA fatigue attack using the stolen credentials of an Uber EXT contractor.

articles.title: Kazakh ransomware hacking suspect extradited from Italy
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The U.S. accused Roman Khlynovskiy of participating in ransomware attacks against healthcare organizations, schools and companies as part of the "8 Digits Team" connected with INC and Lynx.
articles.full_text:
Kazakh ransomware hacking suspect extradited from Italy
An affiliate of the INC and Lynx ransomware strains appeared in a Tennessee court on Monday after being extradited from Italy.
Roman Khlynovskiy, a 43-year-old from Kazakhstan, is accused of launching ransomware attacks against U.S. schools, hospitals and companies.
Khlynovskiy is facing a maximum penalty of 27 years in prison on computer fraud, money laundering, wire fraud, extortion and identity theft charges.
Prosecutors accused him of being a member of a cybercriminal group called the “8-Digits Team” that launched ransomware attacks on behalf of the larger INC and Lynx ransomware gangs.
The team’s cyber intrusions led to $500 million in ransom demands and they claimed to have stolen 50 terabytes of data consisting of more than 70 million confidential health records.
FBI director Kash Patel said U.S. agencies worked with Italian law enforcement to extradite Khlynovskiy.
“The defendant is charged with participating in one of the largest healthcare data breaches in decades,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva. “The indictment alleges a conspiracy that targeted hospitals and healthcare providers, stole vast quantities of sensitive patient information, and then sought to profit by threatening some of the most vulnerable members of our society. These alleged crimes exploited the deeply personal medical information of millions of people.”
Khlynovskiy made his first federal court appearance in Knoxville, Tennessee, on Monday.
Members of the 8-Digits Team attacked companies in at least six states, often targeting schools and hospitals. The hackers breached networks, stole data and extorted victims, demanding payments in exchange for not publishing the data.
The INC ransomware gang took credit for a 2024 ransomware attack on prominent Michigan healthcare system McLaren Health Care — which was forced to cancel dozens of surgeries and operate without critical digital systems for days.
The group also caused chaos last year with an attack on the Dutch conglomerate behind several major U.S. supermarket brands.
The INC gang emerged in 2023 and attacked the State Bar of Texas, Yamaha Motor and printer manufacturer Xerox.
According to Palo Alto Networks and Group-IB, INC either rebranded to Lynx or Lynx actors purchased the group’s source code.
Jonathan Greig

articles.title: Chinese state group developing automated attack tool for cyber espionage, Google says
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Google released its latest AI Threat Tracker report on Monday, writing that threat actors are rapidly evolving their use of artificial intelligence in attacks — now leaning more heavily on autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks like Artex, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI and PentAGI to execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity.
articles.full_text:
Chinese state group developing automated attack tool for cyber espionage, Google says
Both criminal and state-backed groups in China are leveraging AI tools for cyber espionage, vulnerability research and social media influence operations.
Google released its latest AI Threat Tracker report on Monday, writing that threat actors are rapidly evolving their use of artificial intelligence in attacks — now leaning more heavily on autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks like Artex, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI and PentAGI to execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity.
While multiple countries — including Russia, Iran and North Korea — are using AI for nefarious purposes, few countries have matched China.
Google researchers said they saw Chinese state-backed and financially motivated actors using AI tools for “reconnaissance, front-end scanning, researching targets across various sectors and geographies, and weaponizing exploits.”
Incident responders saw Chinese contractors using large language models to translate and comb through tranches of stolen data that were eventually organized and sold to customers. Other Chinese actors are using AI platforms’ file-hosting infrastructure to stage archives of phishing lures and exfiltrate stolen data.
Several different Chinese actors are also experimenting heavily with Artex — which was spotlighted on Friday by the FBI in an alert that drew alarm among cybersecurity experts. The tool was created by a Chinese researcher and allows any user to turn a large language model into a powerful hacking tool that can “automate multiple phases of cyber intrusions at machine speed, from reconnaissance through data exfiltration,” according to the FBI.
Google said it found evidence that Chinese government groups are now developing their own version of Artex for “likely use in cyber espionage operations.”
While Artex has garnered the most media coverage, Google said they have seen similar tools used in real attacks or tested by threat actors in private — including CAIRN, PentAGI, CyberStrikeAI and HexStrike AI.
CAIRN allows AI agents to collaborate on breaching targets, often starting with a target’s IP address and ending with an operational objective. Google saw CAIRN used in intrusions of companies in the U.S. aerospace sector.
Some threat actors used PentAGI to conduct “systematic reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning against a wide range of organizations in Asia,” the researchers added.
Vulnerability research and disinformation
Google said multiple countries and vendors now routinely employ large language models to research new bugs, create fake content, manipulate SEO and generate influence content.
The report cites one instance of Iranian government-backed actor APT42 using several large language models, including Google’s Gemini, to conduct targeted reconnaissance and social engineering attacks.
North Korea has continued to deploy AI to support its IT worker campaign, using it to create resumes and supplement knowledge during job interviews.
The researchers added that recent intrusions into cryptocurrency organizations in North America and Europe saw North Korean hackers use AI to create fake recruiter profiles on professional networking profiles.
The fictitious personas then conducted ClickFix attacks — where hackers force victims to take actions on their device to fix problems that are not real. The tactic has been used widely by North Korean actors in multiple attacks on cryptocurrency companies and was recently spotlighted as part of a long-running campaign recently disrupted by the FBI.
Google found another version of the scheme, with North Korean actors conducting ClickFix attacks and breaching a victim’s device, allowing them to pivot into internal code repositories to install code directly into the large language models the companies use.
The hackers modified code so that when users started up Claude Code, it would automatically trigger the download of a backdoor researchers call SOMBERMEME.
Threat actors are also using LLMs to automate labor- and time-intensive phases of vulnerability analysis, allowing them to quickly analyze patches to find bugs — dramatically reducing the window between patch disclosure and exploitation.
Google said zero-day exploits rose significantly this year, going from eight per month in 2025 to 22 in the month of August.
As an example, Google cited two vulnerabilities that emerged this summer affecting PaperCut print management servers. Researchers were able to generate working exploits for the bug within a day of their disclosure using LLMs.
Researchers noted in their report that while AI tools have compressed attack timelines and allowed some threat actors to move at “machine speed,” they do generate significant forensic traffic and rely on recognizable identifiers, leaving behind distinct code-level traces.
“While these artifacts increase the likelihood of detection and mitigation, these tools remain highly capable of achieving operational objectives,” Google said. “As the sophistication of these tools and underlying LLMs increases, we anticipate not only reduced human involvement in these operations but also increased stealth and sophistication of the activity.”
Jonathan Greig
is a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.
